description: Development of a space mission simulation game
summary:
Lactomeda is a browser pixel-art game in which students aged 13–17 design a NASA-style space mission and
then fly it. Players pick a mission and set its science targets. They build the spacecraft and choose
instruments, an orbit, a rocket and ground stations, trading off mass, power, budget, data, comms and
time. Then they walk inside the ship they built and keep it alive through emergencies. The design steps
follow real NASA practice: JPL Concept Maturity Levels, a Goddard Mission Design Lab–style review and
orbit data computed with NASA GMAT
details:
PROJECT DESCRIPTION

What it does

Lactomeda turns the mission design process into a game with two halves. The game is available in English and Spanish.

1. Design

- The player chooses one of three missions: Student CubeSat, Wildfire Watch or Space Telescope. Then they choose a difficulty: Cadet, Engineer or Flight Director.

- Beginners can start from a working starter spacecraft. On Cadet they can also use recommended targets and let the game pick the background parts (structure, thermal, computer, attitude) for their bus.

- Each objective has threshold, baseline and goal levels, and the player picks one for each.

- The player builds the spacecraft from a short, curated list:

- a 3U CubeSat, a SmallSat or a large bus, with parts for 8 subsystems;

- 6 instruments;

- 4 orbits with an altitude slider;

- 4 launchers, including the free NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative;

- 3 ground networks.

- A live resource bar shows the margin of each of the six resources: green, amber or red.

- A concept maturity meter rises from CML 1 to CML 4.

- The phase ends with a design review modelled on a Mission Design Lab study. It gives one finding per discipline, an equipment list and cost, and a GO / NO-GO launch decision. A mission with no instrument cannot launch.

2. Flight

- A pixel-art launch animation shows the real launch phases: countdown, Max Q, stage and fairing separation, then orbit insertion. A launch can fail, and then the game shows a lesson from a real NASA mishap.

- In orbit, the player walks a ship generated from their design, with one room and console per subsystem.

- Emergencies flash at the stations. The player walks to the station and chooses an option, such as repair, switch to the backup or safe mode. Each option shows its cost.

- Ignored alarms can turn into worse events.

- Optional station tasks earn extra rewards, and skipping them costs nothing.

- A flight HUD shows the mission day, progress, resources and part health.

3. Debrief

- The score out of 1000 is split into five bars: science, mission goals, room to spare, parts that kept working and alarms answered in time.

- The stars and the outcome are shown.

- "The 3 most important things" gives what went well, what went wrong and a tip for next time.

- After a failed launch, the debrief shows the cause and the lesson engineers learned.

- "Fly again" restores the design, shows what changed and lets the player replay the same emergencies or get new ones.

Team mode lets up to 4 players join a room with a 6-letter code and take mission roles: Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Payload Scientist and Flight Ops & Comms. With fewer players, roles are merged.

How it works

- It is a web app made with React and TypeScript, with a Phaser pixel-art scene for the ship and flight.

- The simulation engine is made of pure, deterministic functions, so the same seed always gives the same flight. The engine covers mass, power (with eclipse and degradation), link budget, data, cost, delta-v and propellant, lifetime, objectives, launch outcome, the emergency deck and the end-of-mission explanation. It is covered by unit tests.

- All game content is stored in JSON files, and each catalog entry has a "ref" field that names its source.

- All interface text goes through i18next. There are English and Spanish files, and a test checks that both have the same keys and placeholders.

- Team rooms use Supabase realtime presence.

- The game runs in any modern browser with nothing to install. It is deployed on Vercel.

Benefits

- Students learn by doing that every engineering choice has a cost. For example, a sharper camera means more data, which needs more contact time and more power.

- The steps, words and review format are the ones NASA teams use, so the game also introduces real mission design vocabulary.

- The game uses real numbers: imaging geometry is checked against Landsat 8/9 and VIIRS, and the LEO orbit values come from a NASA GMAT run.

- The game is built for beginners: starter spacecraft, recommended targets, short choice lists, readable text and a Spanish version.

- Failure is part of learning: the debrief explains the score and gives a tip. "Fly again" then invites students to change one thing and try again.

What we hope to achieve

We want students who have never seen a mission design study to come away understanding how missions are planned, why trade-offs matter, and how the people on a mission team work together. We also hope it makes them want to take part in real student CubeSat programmes such as NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative.

USE OF NASA DATA AND RESOURCES

- Design and Develop Science Missions: the four mission segments (launch, space, ground, user) organise the design tabs and the mission report.

- GMAT: we wrote a GMAT script (gmat/leo500.script) and ran it in GMAT R2025a. It covered 7 days, 500 km altitude, 51.6° inclination and a ground station in San José, Costa Rica. It gave a 94.6 min period, about 35 min of eclipse per orbit and 3.1 passes per day. Those values feed the LEO orbit and its power and comms budgets, and the orbit card says "Computed with NASA GMAT".

- JPL Concept Maturity Levels: the design phases are CML 1–4, shown on a maturity meter.

- Goddard Mission Design Lab: the design review gives one finding per discipline, an equipment list, cost and a GO / NO-GO decision. The ship's rooms are the same disciplines.

- CubeSat 101 / NASA CSLI: it gives the Student CubeSat scenario and its starter spacecraft, the CubeSat unit sizes and masses, the university ground station and the free CSLI launch option.

- A Learning Game About Telescopes: the wavelength rules decide which instruments fit each objective.

- NASA Mission Viz: linked in the game's NASA Sources screen; it inspired the launch and orbit visuals.

- Visualize a Space Mission Using VR (Space Apps 2023): its concept → trajectory → timeline structure shapes the launch timeline and the flight HUD.

- Other NASA data: the multispectral imager matches Landsat 8/9 OLI (30 m, 185 km swath), and the fire-detection camera is modelled on VIIRS (Suomi NPP / NOAA-20). Part values come from NASA's State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, the MMRTG fact sheet, the DSN Link Design Handbook and the SLS fact sheet. Launch lessons come from the NASA mishap summaries for OCO, Glory and CRS-7.

- An in-game NASA Sources screen lists every challenge resource, what it does in the game and where to see it.

SPACE AGENCY PARTNER RESOURCES

- Canadian Space Agency — Digital Games and Activities: our model for short, kid-friendly explanations in tooltips and on the NASA Sources screen.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Phaser 4, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, i18next (English and Spanish), seedrandom, Supabase, Vitest, oxlint, NASA GMAT R2025a, Python (GMAT output parser), Node.js (sprite generator), Git and GitHub, Jira, Vercel.

USE OF AI

The team used Claude (Anthropic) and Claude Code as coding and writing assistants. They helped write code, tests and documentation. All game design decisions, scientific choices and code reviews were made by the team, and every change was reviewed by a team member before merging.
